task: check the status of a case or application (passport application status, USCIS case status, job-application portals): locate the status-check page, enter the case or application identifiers, read the returned status, and interpret what it means and what happens next; complete when the status result is on screen and read. Surface pinned: the agency's or employer's web status portal. Variants: filing the application itself, and contacting the agency about the case, do not belong.

tree.label: Check a case or application status
tree.note: the user goes through 1 and then 2 on every lookup. the user goes through 3 if the status only shows inside an account or they want alerts - on the employer portal and on Passport Seva's account route the login in 3.3 replaces 4.5, and on USCIS the user also adds the case in 3.4. the user then goes through 4 and 5; after 5.3 and 5.4 the user goes back to 1.6, 4.3 or 4.6 until a result loads, or decides to wait. once a status is on screen the user goes through 6. after reading the status the user goes on to 7, and to 7.6 only when the status says dispatched or the agency names a courier.

children.label: Reach the status portal
children.note: the user reaches a site through one of 1.1, 1.2 or 1.3. after any search the user goes through 1.4, then 1.5 if they choose to. on a provider that serves several countries or agencies the user goes through 1.6, before or after 1.4. the user goes through 1.7 whenever a popup or a banner appears - when first opening the site, and again inside an account.

questions.question: Does the search need the country name to reach the right page?
questions.why: The browser's autocomplete suggestions indicate that including the specific destination country alongside the agency name is necessary to find the exact tracking portal.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the assurance that the agent will search for the correct country-specific portal rather than getting lost on a generic agency page.
questions.check: Do the search suggestions or results show a separate tracking page per country, so the country name has to be in the query?
questions.say_example: This agency has a page for each country. Putting <the destination country> in the search to reach the right one.

questions.question: Is the address in the bar the agency's own site, not a look-alike?
questions.why: Entering the exact official URL in the address bar ensures you navigate directly to the legitimate government site rather than relying on potentially deceptive search results.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally verify that your sensitive case information is being entered into the official government domain rather than a third-party phishing site.
questions.check: Does the address bar show the agency's genuine domain, not a look-alike or unofficial one?
questions.say_example: That address isn't <agency.gov>. It's <agency-status.com>, a different site. Going to the real one.

children.label: Follow the link in the notice

questions.question: Is the result being clicked the agency's own tracking page, not a paid listing?
questions.why: The search results display multiple options and suggestions for 'vfs tracking', requiring you to identify the official VFS Global link.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to ensure the agent selects the official tracking portal rather than a third-party or phishing site.
questions.check: Does the clicked result's address belong to the agency's own domain, rather than a sponsored or third-party listing?
questions.say_example: That result is a paid listing, not the agency's own site. Going to the official one.

questions.question: Is the top result the tracker, or is the right one further down the list?
questions.why: The first result is the official government site, but the second result specifically mentions tracking a passport via US Travel Docs, which is the required regional portal.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to ensure the agent selects the specific regional tracking service rather than defaulting to the first official government link.
questions.check: Is the correct tracking portal the top government result, or an official regional portal lower down the list?
questions.say_example: The top result is the general government site. The tracker for your region is further down. Using that one.

questions.question: Is this site charging a fee to check the status?
questions.why: Search engines often feature sponsored results for commercial services that charge unnecessary fees to check or 'expedite' statuses that official government sites provide for free.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to avoid unnecessary charges and protect your payment information from predatory third-party services masquerading as official channels.
questions.check: Does the page ask for a payment or fee to check the status, rather than offering it for free?
questions.say_example: This site wants <a fee> just to check the status. The agency's own site does it for free. Going back to that one.

questions.question: Is this the agency's own site, on a secure connection?
questions.why: Verifying the Department of Homeland Security header and the secure uscis.gov URL ensures you are not entering sensitive immigration details into a fraudulent phishing site.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the peace of mind that comes from personally verifying the site's security indicators before handing over your private case numbers.
questions.check: Does the page show the official domain, a secure connection, and the agency's own header or seal?
questions.say_example: This is the agency's own site, <agency>.gov. The connection is secure and the page carries the government header.

questions.question: Is this portal for the country the application was filed for?
questions.why: The screen specifies this portal is specifically for the Embassy of Ireland in the Philippines, meaning you must ensure this matches your actual application destination to retrieve the correct status.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose the ability to verify that the agent is checking your status on the exact country-specific portal where your application was submitted.
questions.check: Does the country named on this portal match the country the application was filed for, including when a lookup has just been rejected?
questions.say_example: This portal covers <a different country> from your application. Switching to the right one.

questions.question: Which of this site's trackers covers your application?
questions.why: The dropdown menu requires selecting the destination country to ensure the status query retrieves the correct application.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to verify that the agent is checking the application status for the correct destination country.
questions.check: Does the site have a separate tracker for each country, office or filing date, and is it not yet known which one covers this application?
questions.say_example: This site has a separate tracker for each country. Which country's visa are you checking?

questions.question: Does the page show a notice about delays, reduced hours, or a closed office?
questions.why: The orange banner highlights recent updates and center re-openings for Atlanta, San Francisco, and New York that might affect application processing.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to proactively learn about regional service disruptions that could explain delays in your application's status.
questions.verify_form: The agent skipped or opened the orange banner about the centres - check which; a closed centre is the reason a status has not moved.
questions.check: Does the page show a notice about service disruptions, reduced capacity, a centre re-opening, or the office being closed with processing suspended?
questions.say_example: There's a notice about <the office handling your file>. It's running at reduced hours. That could be why the status hasn't moved.

children.label: Find the status tool
children.note: the user goes through 2.1 on every lookup, and 2.2 wherever two services sit side by side. if the portal asks questions before it shows a form, the user answers them in 2.3. if a notice blocks the form, the user accepts it in 2.4. before the first lookup the user checks in 2.5 when a status becomes available, where the page says so - on jQSk that check is the third question.

questions.question: Is this the status tool itself, or a neighbouring service like processing times or appointments?
questions.why: The homepage offers multiple services and tools, such as scheduling appointments or finding offices, so you must identify the specific icon for tracking an application.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user misses the chance to see other available immigration services and tools that might be relevant to their broader situation.
questions.check: Is the page the agent opened actually the status-check tool, rather than a neighbouring service like processing times or appointments?
questions.say_example: This is the <Processing Times> page, not the status tool. Going back to the right one.

questions.question: Is this the login for applicants, not the one for employees?
questions.why: The screen presents distinct login options for employees, recruiting candidates, and contractors, so you must choose the correct path to find your application.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to ensure the agent categorizes your account correctly to access the appropriate portal.
questions.check: Is the selected login the one for applicants, rather than for employees or contractors?
questions.say_example: That's the employee login. You're checking your own application, so switching to the candidate one.

questions.question: Is the selected tab the one for a pending application, not a visa already issued?
questions.why: The text overlay promises to track a visa application, but clicking the 'File Validity' tab checks an already issued visa instead of a pending application.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses accurate tracking of their pending application if the agent checks the wrong system tab.
questions.check: Does the selected tab track a pending application, rather than looking up an already-issued visa?
questions.say_example: That tab looks up visas already issued. Yours is still pending, so switching to the tracking tab.

questions.question: What does this tool say it can show about the visa?
questions.why: The overview text explains exactly what visa details, such as expiry date and period of stay, the VEVO system can verify.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the context of what specific visa conditions and details the system is capable of showing them.
questions.check: Does the page's overview state which visa details it can show, such as expiry date or period of stay?
questions.say_example: Read the overview - this tool shows <visa class, grant date and expiry date>

questions.question: Is the individual portal selected, rather than the organisation one?
questions.why: The screen presents options for both individuals and organizations, so you must choose the correct path to access your personal visa details.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to ensure the agent correctly navigates to the individual portal rather than an organizational one.
questions.check: Is the individual portal selected, rather than the organisation portal, when checking a personal visa?
questions.say_example: That's the organisation portal. This is your own visa, so switching to the individual one.

questions.question: What does this tracker need to know about how you filed the application?
questions.why: The status portal requires you to select whether you applied inside or outside of Canada or the US to retrieve your application.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to ensure the correct geographical region is selected for your specific application.
questions.check: Does the tracker ask where the application was filed, or how it was sent, before it will search, and are those answers not already known?
questions.say_example: This tracker needs to know how you filed it before it can search. In person or by mail, and roughly when?

questions.question: Does the disclaimer say how long results take to appear?
questions.why: The screen requires you to confirm you understand the 5 to 10 business day waiting period and daily update schedule before checking your status.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the awareness of the specific processing timelines and privacy terms applied to your application data.
questions.verify_form: The agent clicked I have read and understand - check that it also read the waiting rule on that page (5 business days in person, 10 by mail) before expecting a status.
questions.check: Does the page state a waiting period (such as 5 to 10 business days) before results appear, alongside the terms it asks you to accept?
questions.say_example: Accepted the terms - results take <5 to 10 business days> to appear

questions.question: Was the agreement box ticked without the notices being read first?
questions.why: The screen at 01:30 explicitly instructed you to read the Privacy and Computer Fraud and Abuse Acts Notices before checking the box to proceed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the assurance of knowing exactly what legal terms and data privacy conditions are being accepted on your behalf.
questions.verify_form: The agent ticked the box saying it read the privacy and fraud notices - check whether the notices were ever opened.
questions.check: Was the agreement box checked without the Privacy and Computer Fraud and Abuse Acts notices ever being opened, even though the page instructed reading them first?
questions.say_example: The page asks you to read the notices first. They weren't. Reading them now before ticking the box.

questions.question: Does this disclaimer page carry any of your details yet, or is the real form next?
questions.why: The screen presents 'SUBMIT' and 'CANCEL' buttons, requiring a choice to finalize and send the status query.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the final opportunity to review their entered identifiers and cancel the request before submitting it to the agency.
questions.verify_form: The agent clicked SUBMIT on the disclaimer page - check that this page carried no personal data yet and that the next page is the form itself.
questions.check: Does this page carry any personal data yet, or is it only the disclaimer before the actual form?
questions.say_example: Submitted the disclaimer page - no personal details sent yet

questions.question: How long after the package arrives before the tracker shows anything?
questions.why: The email from VFS confirms receipt of your package and explains that you must wait two to three business days before the online tracking system will reflect your status.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the direct reassurance of reading the email confirmation that your physical documents safely arrived and understanding the specific timeline for when online tracking becomes active.
questions.check: Does the confirmation email shown on screen state the package was received, and give a waiting period before online tracking shows anything?
questions.say_example: The email says your package arrived. The tracker won't show anything for <two to three business days> yet.

questions.question: Does the portal say how long before a new application appears online?
questions.why: Mailed or recently submitted applications often take weeks to be ingested into the tracking database, meaning a 'Not Found' result requires checking the agency's stated timeline rather than assuming the package was lost.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the context that your application is simply in the standard pre-ingestion waiting period, leading to unnecessary panic or duplicate submissions.
questions.check: Does the portal state a minimum time before a new application appears online, which would explain a 'Not Found' result?
questions.say_example: The portal says applications take <a few weeks> to appear online. So <Not Found> may just mean it's too soon.

children.label: Use the account route
children.note: the user goes through 3.1 if they choose to use an account or the portal offers nothing else. for a new account the user also goes through 3.2, once. the user goes through 3.3 each time they use the account. on USCIS the user then adds the case by its number in 3.4; on portals that already list the application - Passport Seva's account and the employer portal - the user goes through 3.5 instead. from 3.4 or 3.5 the user goes straight to 6.

questions.question: Do you want me to set up an account in your name to track this case?
questions.why: The page displays a 'SIGN UP' button and recommends creating an account to easily track cases and receive text or email alerts.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the choice of whether to share the additional personal information required to create a permanent tracking account.
questions.verify_form: The agent started a sign-up for a tracking account or stayed on the public tool - check which; the sign-up asks for your name, address, email and phone.
questions.check: Does the page offer creating a new account in the person's name to track the case and receive alerts, whether before the lookup or alongside the status once it is shown?
questions.say_example: I can sign up for an account under your name to track this and send alerts, or just check the status now as a guest. Which do you want?

children.label: Create the account
children.note: the user goes through 3.2.1, 3.2.2, 3.2.3 and 3.2.4 in the form's own order, then 3.2.5 before 3.3 - the username in the email is the one the user needs to log in.

questions.question: Were the site's terms read before they were accepted?
questions.why: The screen displays legally binding terms covering your liability, security, and text message notifications that you are agreeing to by clicking 'ACCEPT'.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to review and make an informed decision about the legal obligations and privacy terms being accepted on your behalf.
questions.verify_form: The agent clicked ACCEPT on the myUSCIS terms - check whether it scrolled through them or straight past; those terms cover your liability and the text-message alerts, and nobody read them on your behalf.
questions.check: Were the terms and conditions scrolled or read before Accept was clicked?
questions.say_example: Accepted the site's terms without reading them first. They cover liability and text alerts.

questions.question: Does the account type selected match checking your own case?
questions.why: The portal requires you to choose between an Applicant/Petitioner or Representative role to proceed with account creation.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to ensure the account is legally registered under the correct role for your specific relationship to the application.
questions.check: Is the selected account type Applicant/Petitioner, matching checking your own case, rather than Representative?
questions.say_example: That's the Representative account type. You're checking your own case, so Applicant/Petitioner is the right one.

questions.question: Which fields does the profile form mark as required?
questions.why: The screen requires specific personal information like name and city but marks others as optional, forcing a choice about what data to invent and what to omit.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses control over the specific alias and contact details used to represent their identity in the portal.
questions.verify_form: The agent filled the profile form - check every required value against your real details and which optional fields it skipped; the tutorial typed fake ones and yours must not be.
questions.check: Does the form mark some fields, such as name and city, as required and others as optional?
questions.say_example: Filled in <name and city> - the form marks those required. Left <middle name> blank

questions.question: Does the password being set meet the site's stated rules?
questions.why: The screen displays a 'Security Information' form with a tooltip detailing strict password restrictions that must be met to proceed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to choose memorable login credentials and manage them according to your own personal security habits.
questions.verify_form: The agent set a username and a password for the new account - check that you know both and that the password meets the popup's rules (8 to 14 characters, no dollar sign, expires after 30 days); if the agent invented them, you cannot log in later.
questions.check: Does the password entered meet the page's stated rules for length and allowed characters?
questions.say_example: Setting a password you'll be able to remember, since you're the one signing in later. It fits the site's rule of <8 to 14 characters, no dollar sign>.

questions.question: Which security questions does the account use for recovery?
questions.why: The screen requires selecting four password hint questions and typing answers to verify your identity in case of password loss.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to choose personal security questions and answers that only you would easily remember for future account recovery.
questions.verify_form: The agent picked four security questions and typed answers - check that you would give the same answers; they are the recovery route for this account.
questions.check: Does the account form require security questions and answers used for password recovery?
questions.say_example: Answered the four recovery questions with your own answers, not made-up ones.

questions.question: Did the account actually get created?
questions.why: The screen confirms the myUSCIS account was created, making it important to verify the notification email arrived so you can reliably track your receipt numbers.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the peace of mind of personally verifying that your email is correctly linked to your new immigration case tracking account.
questions.check: Does the page confirm the account was created, and does a confirmation email appear on screen?
questions.say_example: The page confirms your account is created. Watch your inbox for the confirmation email.

questions.question: What username does the confirmation email give?
questions.why: The email explicitly displays your assigned username, which is required to log in and check your case status.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose direct knowledge of your assigned login credentials and the personal confirmation that your account was successfully created.
questions.check: Does the confirmation email state the username that was assigned?
questions.say_example: Read the username <ab[account number]5> from the confirmation email.

questions.question: Does the username being typed match the one in the confirmation email exactly?
questions.why: The screen shows a longer username being typed than the truncated version provided in the confirmation email, which will likely result in a login error.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to catch system-truncated credentials and adjust their login attempts accordingly.
questions.check: Does the username being typed at login match the exact one shown in the confirmation email, without truncation?
questions.say_example: The email shows <ab[account number]5>. A longer version is being typed. That mismatch would fail the sign-in.

questions.question: Which sign-in details should I use for this portal?
questions.why: The portal requires the specific personal email address and password used during the recruiting process to access the dashboard.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to keep your personal login credentials private when authenticating to view your application status.
questions.check: Does the portal require an email address and password to sign in, and are those not already known?
questions.say_example: This needs the email and password you used when you applied. What should I use?

questions.question: Which sign-in method does the page offer?
questions.why: The login screen requires choosing between a password or an OTP to verify your identity and access the portal.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to choose their preferred authentication method and handle the secure OTP themselves.
questions.verify_form: The agent chose the password or the one-time code to log in - check which; the code goes to your registered email and only you can read it.
questions.check: Does the login screen offer both a password option and a one-time-code option?
questions.say_example: Signed in with a password rather than a one-time code.

questions.question: What is the one-time code the site just sent you?
questions.why: The portal requires a time-sensitive OTP sent to your registered email address to authenticate your session, meaning you must have active access to that inbox to proceed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you must either give the agent access to your personal email or coordinate in real-time to hand over the OTP before it expires.
questions.verify_form: The agent asked for a one-time code - check how it got the code out of your inbox and that the code was used before it expired.
questions.check: Does the page say a one-time code was sent, and show a field for entering it?
questions.say_example: The site just sent a one-time code to your <email>. What does it say?

questions.question: Does the action being clicked show the existing case, rather than start a new filing?
questions.why: The dashboard presents multiple options like filing a new form or adding a paper-filed case, so you must choose the correct path to access your case history.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose the awareness of other available account features, such as filing a new form online or entering a representative passcode.
questions.check: Does the selected dashboard action open the existing case's status, rather than starting a new filing?
questions.say_example: That starts a new application. Your existing case is under <View Case Status>. Going there instead.

questions.question: Which receipt number should I use to link your existing case to the account?
questions.why: The portal requires a specific receipt number to successfully link and track your immigration petition.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to verify that the exact receipt number for your application is the one being linked to your profile.
questions.check: Does linking the existing case to the account require a receipt number, and is that number not already known?
questions.say_example: To pull up your existing case I need its receipt number. It usually starts with three letters, like <WAC>. What is it?

questions.question: Is the page still on adding the case, rather than the notification settings?
questions.why: The 'My Cases' page allows you to either manually add a specific application using its receipt number or manage mobile and email alerts for updates.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide exactly how you want to track your case and receive future status updates.
questions.verify_form: The agent entered a receipt number to add a case, or went to the notification settings instead - check which happened; the page offers both and only one links your case.
questions.check: Did the agent stay on adding the case by receipt number, rather than switching to notification settings?
questions.say_example: That's the notification settings page. Going back to add the case by its receipt number.

questions.question: Which method does the dashboard offer for linking an existing case?
questions.why: The dashboard displays different methods for linking an application, such as adding a paper-filed case, which determines how the system retrieves your status.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to specify how your application was originally filed, which might be necessary to successfully link the case to your account.
questions.check: Which method did the dashboard offer for adding the case, such as paper-filed versus standard entry?
questions.say_example: Linked the case using the <paper-filed> option, matching how it was actually submitted.

questions.question: Should the case stay linked to the account after the status is read?
questions.why: The dashboard provides a 'Remove' link next to the case, allowing you to unlink the receipt number from this specific account if you only wanted to perform a one-time check.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to keep your case history disconnected from the agent's account if they fail to remove the case after checking it.
questions.verify_form: The agent left the case in the account or clicked Remove - check which; removing it ends the alerts.
questions.check: Does the dashboard offer a Remove link that would unlink the case and stop its alerts?
questions.say_example: Leaving the case linked so the alerts keep coming. Say the word if you'd rather I remove it.

children.label: Enter the identifiers
children.note: the user goes through 4.1 first on every form. 4.2 and 4.3 where the form asks the kind before the value. the user goes through 4.4 when they do not have the number - in most videos they leave the portal to find it. then 4.5 and 4.6 together, 4.7 and 4.8 as the form asks, 4.9 where a captcha sits on the form, and 4.10 before 5. on the account route 4.5 and 4.6 happen inside 3.4, and on the employer portal the user skips this goal.

questions.question: What does this site need from you before it can look up the status?
questions.why: The screen explicitly lists the required personal details, such as your date of birth and the last four digits of your Social Security Number, needed to use the online system.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally review exactly what sensitive personal information is required to access your application status.
questions.check: Does the page state which details are needed before searching - such as a reference or token number, a date of birth, or the last four digits of a Social Security Number?
questions.say_example: This site needs your <date of birth> and the last four digits of your <Social Security Number> to look this up.

questions.question: Does the form ask for different details than the site's instructions said?
questions.why: The tracking instructions stated to use your last name, but the actual form required a Date of Birth instead.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to troubleshoot the discrepancy and provide the alternative personal information needed to check the status.
questions.check: Does the form's actual required field differ from what the earlier instructions said to use?
questions.say_example: The instructions said last name. The form is actually asking for date of birth. Going with what the form asks for.

questions.question: Does the application type selected match the kind of application actually filed?
questions.why: The form requires selecting the specific passport service type, such as reissuance or new passport, to proceed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to specify the exact passport service they applied for, which might be necessary to retrieve the correct application status.
questions.check: Does the application type on the form, including the page's own default, match the kind of application actually filed, such as new versus reissue?
questions.say_example: This is set to <reissue>, but yours was a <new passport>. Changing it before searching.

questions.question: Does the interview location selected match where the interview happened?
questions.why: The status portal requires selecting the specific interview location from a dropdown menu to locate the correct application record.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the assurance that the correct interview city is selected, which is required to successfully retrieve your specific case status.
questions.check: Does the selected interview location match where the actual interview took place?
questions.say_example: This is set to <a different city> from where the interview was. Correcting it.

questions.question: Do the search method and document type match how this application should be looked up?
questions.why: The 'File Validity' form requires you to choose a search method, such as 'Passport Information', and a document type, such as 'Visa', to determine what identifiers you must provide next.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide which of your personal identifiers, such as your passport details versus a file number, are used to retrieve your immigration status.
questions.check: Do the selected search method and document type match how the actual application should be looked up?
questions.say_example: This is set to search by <file number>, but the number on hand is a <passport number>. Switching the search method.

questions.question: Does the identifier type selected match the number actually on hand?
questions.why: The dropdown menu requires you to specify the type of identifier you are providing so the system can correctly locate your record.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide which piece of personal identification is used to retrieve your application status.
questions.check: Does the selected identifier type match the kind of number actually available (such as a receipt number versus a token)?
questions.say_example: This is set to <token number>, but the number on hand is a <receipt number>. Switching it.

questions.question: Are the reference-number options under the dropdown being searched, or a different one?
questions.why: The screen shows the 'Document type' dropdown open while discussing options like TRN and Visa Grant Number, which actually belong in the 'Reference type' dropdown.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance that their application identifiers will be entered correctly if the agent gets stuck searching for options in the wrong dropdown menu.
questions.check: Are the reference-number options (such as TRN or Visa Grant Number) being looked for in the Reference type dropdown, not the Document type dropdown?
questions.say_example: Those options sit under 'Reference type', not 'Document type'. Looking there instead.

questions.question: Does the letter mark any of its numbers as the wrong one to use?
questions.why: The screen shows red crosses over the Group URN and Reference Number on the appointment letter, indicating these specific numbers will cause an error if used for tracking.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to prevent the agent from mistakenly using the invalid reference numbers printed on the appointment letter.
questions.check: Does the appointment letter mark certain numbers, such as a Group URN, as not the one to use?
questions.say_example: The appointment letter crosses out the <Group URN>. That's not the number this form wants.

questions.question: Does the document type selected match the document on hand?
questions.why: The form requires you to choose a specific identification document, such as a Passport or ImmiCard, from the dropdown menu to proceed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to decide which of your valid identification documents is used to look up your visa status.
questions.check: Does the selected identity document type (such as Passport versus ImmiCard) match the document actually on hand?
questions.say_example: This is set to <ImmiCard>, but the document on hand is a <passport>. Switching it.

children.label: Find the number in the notice

questions.question: Where does the token number for this lookup live?
questions.why: The status portal requires a specific token number that was previously emailed to you, prompting you to open the Gmail app from your home screen to find it.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step requires giving an agent access to your personal email inbox, which exposes your private correspondence.
questions.verify_form: The agent went into your email to find the token - check that it opened only the application email and that you are fine with it reading the inbox.

questions.why: Checking that the March 2nd dispatch date and the March 4th delivery date reflect a realistic two-day transit time confirms the status details are consistent.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to personally sanity-check the timeline and catch any logical discrepancies in the processing dates.
questions.check: Do the dispatch date and delivery date shown reflect a plausible transit gap, rather than delivery before dispatch?
questions.say_example: The tracker shows it delivered before it was dispatched. Those two dates can't both be right.

questions.question: Does the tracker's status match what the text message said?
questions.why: The SMS message claims the application was granted without police verification, but the tracker page contradicts this by showing it is pending physical police verification.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to spot a critical contradiction in the agency's communications that likely requires manual follow-up.
questions.check: Does the tracker page's status agree with the text message shown on screen?
questions.say_example: The text message says <granted>. The tracker still shows <a step pending>. Going with the tracker, since it's the live record.

questions.question: Does the page offer a certificate you can download?
questions.why: The screen displays the search-result page with the cursor resting on the 'Certificate' button, presenting the option to download the official status document.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide whether to download the official certificate file to their device or simply read the status on the screen.
questions.verify_form: The agent clicked Certificate or only read the status - check whether a file was downloaded; the certificate is the document you carry.
questions.check: Does the page offer a 'Certificate' (or similarly named) button to download the official status document?
questions.say_example: There's a 'Certificate' button here for the official document. Downloading it now so there's proof on hand.

questions.question: Do the details on the visa grant notice look complete and match the applicant?
questions.why: Checking the applicant details, validity period, and barcode ensures the issued visa is accurate and can be authenticated for travel.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the direct visual confirmation of the official document's details and the barcode used to prove its legitimacy at the border.
questions.check: Do the applicant details, validity period, and barcode on the visa grant notice look complete and match the applicant?
questions.say_example: The <validity period> is missing from this notice. A real grant notice carries one.

questions.question: Do you want to save or print this PDF of your visa conditions before moving on?
questions.why: The screen displays a 3-page PDF with specific work entitlements and mandatory visa conditions that you will likely need to reference later.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to securely save a personal copy of your official visa entitlements and conditions for your own offline records.
questions.verify_form: The agent saved or printed the entitlements PDF, or closed it - check that a copy exists somewhere you can find.
questions.check: Does the page offer a PDF of the visa conditions that has not been saved yet?
questions.say_example: This PDF has the visa conditions on it. Saving it now, since it won't be easy to get back to.

questions.question: Did the status report save straight to the default downloads folder, without asking where to put it?
questions.why: The VEVO results page automatically sends the generated file to the browser's download bar, bypassing any prompt to choose a specific destination.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to immediately organize and rename the sensitive status document into a specific, secure folder on your device.
questions.verify_form: The agent let the PDF land in the default download folder - check where it went; the file holds your visa details.
questions.check: Does the downloaded file land in the browser's default download folder without asking where to save it?
questions.say_example: This saved straight to the default downloads folder. It holds your case details, so move it somewhere private.

children.label: Keep checking afterwards
children.note: the user goes through 7.1 after every status that is not final. 7.2 and 7.3 if they want them - on USCIS, 7.3 is also why the user goes through 3.1. 7.4 whenever a message arrives, with 7.5 before trusting it. 7.6 only when 6.1 says dispatched or the agency names a courier. 7.7 last, on any account route or a shared computer.

questions.question: Does the page say what happens if the status doesn't change online?
questions.why: The tracking page explains that you will receive email or SMS updates, which is important to know if the online portal fails to reflect the current status.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the reassurance of knowing to monitor your email or phone for SMS updates if the online portal remains unchanged.
questions.verify_form: The agent kept refreshing the portal or turned to email and SMS - check which; the tracking page says the decision arrives by email when the portal does not update.
questions.check: Does the page state what will happen if the status doesn't change online (e.g., an email or SMS will be sent instead)?
questions.say_example: The page says you'll get an email or text if nothing changes here. No need to keep refreshing.

questions.question: Do you want text alerts, knowing your carrier may charge for them?
questions.why: The text message alert explicitly states 'Msg and Data Rates May Apply,' meaning you could be charged by your mobile carrier for receiving these automated updates.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to opt out of SMS notifications if you want to avoid potential messaging and data charges from your mobile carrier.
questions.verify_form: The agent turned on text alerts - check that you accept the carrier's message and data charges the alert itself warns about.
questions.check: Does the alert signup page warn that message and data rates may apply?
questions.say_example: The page warns that message and data rates may apply for text alerts. Want me to sign you up anyway?

questions.question: How does the page say updates will reach you?
questions.why: The screen shows a text message alert from USCIS, demonstrating that users can receive automated SMS notifications when their case status changes.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means you might not receive real-time text alerts on your personal device, potentially delaying your awareness of important case updates.
questions.check: Does the page show an example of how notifications will be delivered, such as a sample text message?
questions.say_example: Updates come by text message from the agency, like the example shown here.

questions.question: Does this email's receipt number match the case being tracked?
questions.why: Selecting the correct email from USCIS-CaseStatus ensures you are reading the update associated with your specific receipt number.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the direct reassurance of seeing the official USCIS sender address and verifying firsthand that the update matches your exact receipt number.
questions.check: Does the email's subject or body show the receipt number that matches the one being tracked?
questions.say_example: This email is for receipt <[case-no]>, the one being checked. Reading it now.

questions.question: Is there an email from the agency about the application in the inbox on screen?
questions.why: The inbox shows unrelated emails from MyAccount and Meta Support, confirming no proactive passport updates have been sent.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to manually verify your inbox and decide whether to sign up for future email notifications.
questions.check: Does the inbox show an email from the passport/visa agency about the application, among the visible messages?
questions.say_example: No email from the agency in the inbox yet. Just other, unrelated messages.

questions.question: Is this email from the agency's own address?
questions.why: Checking the sender address for the official '.gov' domain confirms the interview notification is a legitimate government communication.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the peace of mind of personally verifying the email's authenticity and directly reading your interview details.
questions.check: Does the sender's email address use an official government domain matching the agency?
questions.say_example: The sender's address ends in <.gov>. That matches a real government address, not a look-alike.

children.label: Follow the dispatched passport
children.note: the user goes through 7.6.1, then 7.6.2, then 7.6.3. 7.6.2 is 4.5 and 4.6 again on the courier's form, with a postcode or a passport number as the key. 7.6.3 can come back empty, as it does for BZC1.

questions.question: Does the email say where the delivery can be tracked?
questions.why: The email provides a specific TNT tracking URL and reference number to monitor the secure delivery of the passport.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the reassurance of personally reading the official communication that confirms exactly which courier service is handling their sensitive document.
questions.check: Does the email provide a specific tracking website and reference number for the delivery?
questions.say_example: The email points to <the courier's tracking site>, with reference <a tracking number>. Going there next.

questions.question: What formatting does the tracking form ask for?
questions.why: The tracking form requires specific formatting, such as including a space in the postcode and removing the 'PEX' prefix and spaces from the PAN number, to successfully locate the item.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to manually adjust your reference numbers to meet the specific formatting quirks required by the tracking system.
questions.check: Does the tracking form's instructions specify a formatting rule, such as a space in the postcode or removing a prefix from the reference number?
questions.say_example: Entered the postcode with a space and the reference number without its prefix, matching the form's own example.

questions.question: Which of the two references does the tracking form take?
questions.why: The tracking portal requires your postcode and a choice between your PAN number or consignment number to locate the correct item.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide which of your specific tracking identifiers to use for the query.
questions.check: Does the tracking form ask for either of two identifiers (e.g., a PAN number or a consignment number)?
questions.say_example: Used the reference number already on hand for this lookup.

questions.question: When does the tracker say the documents will arrive?
questions.why: Checking the delivery date for the supporting documents freight type tells you exactly when your original materials will be returned.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the immediate reassurance of knowing the specific date your sensitive personal documents will arrive at your address.
questions.check: Does the courier tracker show a scheduled delivery date for the supporting-documents shipment?
questions.say_example: The supporting documents are due <a date>, according to the tracker.

questions.question: Does the tracker show more than one shipment under this reference?
questions.why: The screen displayed two different consignments (Supporting Documents and Passport) under the same PAN number, requiring a choice of which item to track.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to decide whether to check the status of their supporting documents or the passport itself.
questions.verify_form: The agent opened the passport consignment or the supporting documents one - check which; they have different delivery dates.
questions.check: Does the tracker show more than one consignment (e.g., 'Supporting Documents' and 'Passport') under the same reference?
questions.say_example: Checking both shipments under this reference - the passport and the supporting documents

questions.question: Do the passport and document delivery dates differ, as the email said they would?
questions.why: Checking that the tracking shows different delivery dates for the passport and supporting documents confirms the email's statement that they will arrive in separate mailings.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the reassurance of personally cross-referencing the tracking dates to confirm your sensitive supporting documents are safely accounted for.
questions.check: Do the tracker's delivery dates for the passport and the supporting documents differ, matching the email's statement that they arrive separately?
questions.say_example: Passport due <a date>, documents due <a different date>. That matches the email saying they'd come separately.

questions.question: If the portal required signing in, was the account logged out when finished?
questions.why: The video uses a stock animation to advise logging out for security on shared computers rather than showing the actual portal's interface.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent misses the exact visual steps to locate and click the logout button on the actual portal.
questions.check: If an account was signed into for this lookup, does the final page show it was signed out rather than left open?
questions.say_example: Signed out when finished, since this was on a shared computer.
